title: Astronomy and the Night Sky
source_note: Written for HEARTH, August 2026. Covers the solar system, stars, basic cosmology, the southern sky and Matariki. Matariki content follows widely shared accounts (notably Professor Rangi Mātāmua's work); iwi traditions differ, and the questions say so where it matters.

questions.prompt: How many planets are in our solar system?
questions.explanation: Eight planets orbit the Sun; Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.

questions.prompt: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
questions.explanation: Mercury is the innermost planet, whipping around the Sun in just 88 days.

questions.prompt: Which planet is the hottest in the solar system?
questions.explanation: Venus beats Mercury because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat like a runaway greenhouse.

questions.prompt: Why does Mars look red?
choices: Its surface is covered in rusty iron oxide dust
Red algae grow on its surface
questions.explanation: Iron minerals in the Martian dust have rusted, giving the whole planet its red colour.

questions.prompt: Which is the largest planet in our solar system?
questions.explanation: Jupiter is so big that more than 1,300 Earths could fit inside it.

questions.prompt: Which planet is famous for its bright, easily seen rings?
questions.explanation: Saturn's rings are made of countless chunks of ice and rock.

questions.prompt: What happened to Pluto in 2006?
choices: It was destroyed by an asteroid
It was reclassified as a dwarf planet
questions.explanation: Astronomers agreed on a new definition of planet, and Pluto became the most famous dwarf planet.

questions.prompt: What is the Sun?
questions.explanation: The Sun is an ordinary star that just happens to be very close to us.

questions.prompt: How does the Sun make its energy?
choices: By nuclear fusion, squeezing hydrogen into helium
By reflecting light from other stars
questions.explanation: Deep in its core the Sun fuses hydrogen into helium, releasing enormous energy.

questions.prompt: About how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
questions.explanation: Light crosses the 150 million km from the Sun to Earth in about 8 minutes.

questions.prompt: What is a light year?
choices: The time light takes to cross a galaxy
The distance light travels in one year
questions.explanation: A light year measures distance, about 9.5 trillion kilometres.

questions.prompt: What is the nearest star to the Sun?
questions.explanation: Proxima Centauri is about 4.2 light years away, part of the Alpha Centauri system we can see from NZ.

questions.prompt: Roughly how old is the Sun?
questions.explanation: The Sun and the whole solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago.

questions.prompt: What will the Sun eventually become when it runs low on hydrogen fuel?
questions.explanation: In about 5 billion years the Sun will swell into a red giant, then fade to a white dwarf.

questions.prompt: Why do stars appear to twinkle?
choices: Earth's moving atmosphere bends their light
Clouds pass in front of them
questions.explanation: Wobbling air in our atmosphere bends starlight around, which we see as twinkling.

questions.prompt: What is a black hole?
choices: An object with gravity so strong that not even light can escape
questions.explanation: A black hole packs so much mass into so little space that light itself cannot escape its gravity.

questions.prompt: What causes Earth's seasons?
choices: Earth moving closer to and further from the Sun
The tilt of Earth's axis as it orbits the Sun
questions.explanation: Earth is tilted about 23.5 degrees, so each hemisphere leans towards the Sun for part of the year.

questions.prompt: Why is it summer in New Zealand in December?
choices: Earth is closest to the Sun in December
The southern hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun then
The Sun burns hotter in December
New Zealand moves north in summer
questions.explanation: In December the southern half of Earth leans sunward, so we get long hot days while the north shivers.

questions.prompt: How long does Earth take to spin once on its axis?
questions.explanation: One full spin takes about 24 hours, which is why we have day and night.

questions.prompt: How long does Earth take to orbit the Sun once?
questions.explanation: One orbit takes 365 and a quarter days, and the quarter days add up to a leap day every four years.

questions.prompt: About how long is a full cycle of Moon phases, from full moon to full moon?
questions.explanation: The Moon runs through all its phases in about 29 and a half days.

questions.prompt: What mainly causes the ocean tides?
choices: The Moon's gravity pulling on Earth's oceans
questions.explanation: The Moon's gravity (helped by the Sun's) drags the oceans into bulges that we experience as tides.

questions.prompt: What is a solar eclipse?
choices: The Moon passing between the Sun and Earth
Earth passing between the Sun and Moon
questions.explanation: In a solar eclipse the Moon blocks our view of the Sun and casts its shadow on Earth.

questions.prompt: What is a lunar eclipse?
choices: The Moon passing in front of the Sun
Earth's shadow falling on the Moon
questions.explanation: In a lunar eclipse Earth sits between the Sun and Moon, and our shadow turns the Moon a coppery red.

questions.prompt: Where is the asteroid belt?
questions.explanation: Most asteroids orbit in a belt between Mars and Jupiter.

questions.prompt: Which way does a comet's tail point?
choices: Behind it, like a jet trail
questions.explanation: Sunlight and the solar wind blow the tail away from the Sun, whichever way the comet is moving.

questions.prompt: What is a shooting star really?
choices: A star falling out of the sky
A meteor, a bit of space rock burning up in our atmosphere
questions.explanation: Shooting stars are meteors, tiny bits of rock or dust blazing as they hit our atmosphere.

questions.prompt: What do we call a space rock that survives its fall and lands on the ground?
questions.explanation: Once it reaches the ground it is a meteorite; while it burns in the sky it is a meteor.

questions.prompt: What is the name of our galaxy?
questions.explanation: We live in the Milky Way, a spiral galaxy of billions of stars.

questions.prompt: One te reo Māori name for the Milky Way, pictured as a great fish of the sky, is:
questions.explanation: Te Ikaroa, the long fish, stretches across the summer sky (Mangōroa, the long shark, is another name).

questions.prompt: What is the nearest large galaxy to the Milky Way?
questions.explanation: Andromeda is about 2.5 million light years away and is slowly heading our way.

questions.prompt: About how old is the universe, according to the Big Bang theory?
questions.explanation: Evidence points to the universe beginning about 13.8 billion years ago.

questions.prompt: What did astronomer Edwin Hubble discover about distant galaxies?
choices: They are moving away from us, so the universe is expanding
They are all the same size
They are made of dark matter only
questions.explanation: Hubble showed distant galaxies are racing away from us, the key evidence that space is expanding.

questions.prompt: Which famous constellation appears on the New Zealand flag?
questions.explanation: The four red stars on our flag are the Southern Cross, Te Punga, visible all year from NZ.

questions.prompt: What can the Southern Cross help you find at night?
questions.explanation: Extend the long axis of the Cross about four and a half times and you are looking towards due south.

questions.prompt: The bright 'evening star' or 'morning star' is usually not a star at all. What is it?
questions.explanation: Venus outshines every true star, appearing near the Sun at dusk or dawn.

questions.prompt: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon, in 1969?
questions.explanation: Neil Armstrong stepped out first on the Apollo 11 mission, followed by Buzz Aldrin.

questions.prompt: About how long does the International Space Station take to orbit Earth once?
questions.explanation: The ISS zips around Earth roughly every 90 minutes, so its crew see 16 sunrises a day.

questions.prompt: From where in New Zealand does Rocket Lab launch its Electron rockets?
questions.explanation: Rocket Lab launches from Māhia Peninsula on the East Coast, one of the few private launch sites on Earth.

questions.prompt: Which NZ region is famous as an International Dark Sky Reserve for stargazing?
questions.explanation: The Aoraki Mackenzie reserve protects some of the darkest, clearest night skies in the world.

questions.prompt: What is Matariki?
choices: A star cluster whose rising marks the Māori New Year
A planet visible only from NZ
The brightest single star in the sky
A comet that returns every 76 years
questions.explanation: Matariki is a star cluster, and its midwinter rising signals the Māori New Year in many traditions.

questions.prompt: By what other name do astronomers know the Matariki cluster?
questions.explanation: Matariki is the Pleiades, known as the Seven Sisters in Greek stories and Subaru in Japan.

questions.prompt: In the Matariki tradition, how many stars of the cluster are named and honoured?
questions.explanation: Nine stars are honoured, including Matariki herself, Waitī, Waitā, and the wishing star Hiwa-i-te-rangi.

questions.prompt: During Matariki, the star Pōhutukawa is connected with what?
choices: Remembering those who have died in the past year
questions.explanation: Pōhutukawa carries remembrance of loved ones lost since Matariki last rose, a gentle part of the celebration.

questions.prompt: Some iwi mark the Māori New Year by a different star rising, because Matariki is hard to see from their area. Which star?
questions.explanation: Iwi in areas like Whanganui and Taranaki look to Puanga, showing how traditions differ around the motu.
